chapters.title: Introduction: You Must Learn and Benefit from America's 100 Years of Super Winners
chapters.summary: William O'Neil opens not with theory but with a century of charts where super winners — from 1900s General Motors to 1990s America Online — share quantitative footprints before they multiplied. The promise is empirical: by studying 100 years of winners that rose 300 percent plus, you can extract traits that generalize because price is truth that aggregates expectations. The introduction frames the AAII 1998-2009 study where Investors Business Daily's CAN SLIM at 35.3 percent annually versus S&P 3.3 percent is displayed as a cumulative 2,763 percent bar, the credibility anchor reproduced as illustration with source footnote. O'Neil tells his own 1958 origin story buying his first stock, a textile mill where he lost because he chased tip not earnings, then discovering that earnings acceleration preceded every big run he missed. The study method is described: collect leaders at 52-week highs before big runs and backtest earnings, volume, and industry — an illustration shows a spreadsheet with 100 leaders and columns for C, A, N, S, L, I, M that later chapters define. The anecdote of 1962 when he spotted a small cap with 300 percent earnings jump and held through a 20 percent shakeout to triple illustrates discipline. The introduction's tool is the super winner checklist where each letter is yes-no gated, not averaged, meaning failure on one disqualifies despite strength elsewhere. The closing warning is that most investors study losers to avoid mistakes while winners teach more because base rates of winners are rarer and more informative — illustrated as base rate versus noise where studying 100 winners beats 1,000 mediocre charts for insight. This sets the contract: learn American history of winners to repeat process, not to predict next Tesla by story alone. chapters.title: 1. America's Greatest Stock-Picking Secrets
chapters.summary: The secret is that winners are discovered via the CAN SLIM synthesis, not stock tips. O'Neil dissects three secrets revealed by backtesting. First, earnings dominance: every winner had quarterly earnings growth of 18 percent minimum, often 50-100 percent, in the quarter before run, illustrated as earnings bar chart where winner's bar dwarfs peer median. Second, leadership: winners were among top industry group performers, often number one or two in 197 groups, not laggards at discount, a ranking table shows 197 groups sorted by 6-month price performance where leaders dominate future leaders. Third, market direction decides half the battle: three of four stocks follow market, so timing via market direction indicator trims losers even when stock is perfect — an illustration plots follow-through day where volume up 1.5 percent after attempted rally marks new institutional accumulation. Anecdote is Xerox in 1963 where earnings accelerated from 20 to 70 percent and price broke from cup-with-handle on volume three times average, the textbook example reproduced as chart with annotations of handle shakeout at ten percent. O'Neil counters efficient market myth that cheap low P-E laggards offer safety; data shows winners were high P-E at breakout because market pays for acceleration, illustrated as P-E versus subsequent return where low P-E underperforms. The secret's evidence is survivorship-aware: he tracks winners that were also leaders before run versus those that were not, showing leadership predicts better than low price. The chapter closes with the symmetry that amateurs seek secrets in complexity while secrets are simple: earnings, leadership, market — three filters that eliminate ninety percent of ideas, freeing time to study few runners deeply. chapters.title: 2. How to Read Charts Like a Pro and Improve Your Selection and Timing
chapters.summary: Charts are illustrated as investor psychology in price and volume. O'Neil introduces proper base formation: cup-with-handle, double bottom, flat base, and cup without handle, each defined by depth fifteen to thirty percent for cup, handle five to fifteen and drifting down on low volume, duration seven to sixty-five weeks, illustrated as four schematics with recognizable outline. The breakout rule today's breakout needs volume at least fifty percent above average, illustrated as volume histogram spiking at pivot where price crosses handle high plus $0.10; low volume breakout fails sixty percent. Anecdote is Price T. Rowe at 1990 cup where volume at breakout was 280 percent of average and run was 400 percent, reproduced as weekly chart with volume bars. The handle shakeout is psychology: weak hands sell on ten percent dip, institutions accumulate, then supply thin. A second illustration shows faulty bases — too deep forty percent, handle too high, late stage fourth base — that fail eighty percent, a trap table. O'Neil teaches reading via weekly chart not daily to smooth noise, and using relative strength line that rises before price breakout, illustrated as RS line climbing while price flat meaning leadership. The chapter also maps base count: first and second bases succeed, third is caution, fourth is distribution top where institutions sell into strength, illustrated as base stages numbered 1 to 4 along a long uptrend. The tool is checkup where Daily Graphs Online rates chart pattern A to E; C or worse is avoid. The closing discipline is that chart patterns repeat because fear and greed repeat, and reading them reduces selection to few that also have earnings, merging technical timing with fundamental quality — the IBD marriage that CAN SLIM promises. chapters.title: 3. C = Current Big or Accelerating Quarterly Earnings and Sales per Share
chapters.summary: C demands not just growth but acceleration that surprises consensus. The chapter quantifies that super winners averaged 54 percent quarterly earnings growth pre-breakout, with many showing acceleration quarter over quarter — e.g., 20 then 40 then 80 percent — illustrated as accelerating bars versus steady growth where accelerating predicts better. Sales growth must accompany, typically twenty-five percent plus, to prove demand, not accounting; a table shows winners where sales accelerated alongside earnings had 80 percent success versus earnings alone at 50. O'Neil tells the anecdote of 1970s Levitz Furniture where earnings grew 60 percent but sales were flat due to one-time tax credit, and price stalled, proving non-operating earnings mislead. The illustration maps EPS versus sales divergence as red flag. The chapter teaches to check quarterly versus annual: current quarter is leading indicator that annual smoothing hides, illustrated as quarter and annual bars where quarter turns before annual. Screening uses Earnings Per Share Rating where 80 minimum is required — a proprietary percentile versus market — and SMR rating for sales, margin, ROE. An illustration shows Investors.com stock checkup where EPS 95 and SMR A signal pass. The chapter warns against sequential deceleration: three quarters of 30 then 25 then 15 signals supply saturation even if still growing, a deceleration chart where run ends before earnings turn negative. The discipline is to demand both magnitude and direction — up and accelerating — and to avoid value trap where low P-E masks earnings decline, illustrated as price falling despite cheap P-E when C fails. Together C is the first gate where failure vetoes despite perfect chart or story. chapters.title: 4. A = Annual Earnings Increases: Look for Big Growth
chapters.summary: A extends C to annual consistency where three-year earnings growth of twenty-five percent midpoint signals scalable model, not one-off contract. The chapter's database shows winners averaged annual growth 36 percent for three years before run, illustrated as three-year bar where steady climb beats spiky one-hit, a contrast table shows steady versus lumpy success rates. The exception that proves rule is turnaround where three-year looks poor but recent quarters accelerate — O'Neil labels N for new management or product that resets annual — illustrated as U-shaped annual curve where recent quarter inflection predicts breakout despite poor history. Anecdote is Wal-Mart 1980s where annual earnings compounded 30 percent for five years while store count doubled, annual chart shows store count and earnings rising together, proving scalability. The chapter teaches to check ROE at 17 percent plus and pre-tax margins improving, because growth without margin means leverage not efficiency, illustrated as margin expansion where winner's margin widens while laggard's narrows despite sales growth. Return on equity is shown as DuPont-lite where A requires high ROE without excessive debt; a table shows winner ROE 25 at low debt versus leverage ROE 25 at high debt, the former preferred. Screening uses Earnings Per Share Rating that blends quarterly and annual; A complements C where C is quarter and A is year. The chapter's failure case is a construction firm with 100 percent annual growth one year via acquisition, then flat, where growth was financial engineering not organic, chart shows acquisition spike then stall predicting failed base. The discipline is that A must be organic, margin-backed, and multi-year or N must explain why annual resets, preventing growth trap where one good year fools C screen. chapters.title: 5. N = Newer Companies, New Products, New Management, New Highs Off Properly Formed Chart Bases
chapters.summary: N captures that newness fuels price because market underestimates adoption S-curve. The chapter shows that fifty percent of super winners were new issues within ten years and that IPOs with new product often double within first two years — an illustration plots months from IPO to first big base where median is 18 months. The new product illustration shows Apple's iPod in 2001 where quarterly sales chart inflects from flat to triple, preceding price. New management is dramatized via Apple 1997 where Steve Jobs return is marked on chart where price base forms then run — an anecdote where leadership change preceded earnings turn by two quarters, showing management as leading indicator. New highs off properly formed bases is the timing corollary: buy near all-time high off base, not off bottom, because strength indicates institutional accumulation, illustrated as price hugging 52-week high versus laggard at 50 percent below high where subsequent return diverges 300 versus 20 percent. The chapter teaches that old companies can be new again via product: IBM's PC in 1981 or McDonald's McNuggets in 1983 both created N within old, illustrated as product launch markers on long-term charts. Screening uses New High versus New Low list where New High volume leaders are candidates. The failure case is buying old-economy turnarounds without new product where high is not new but rebound — value trap where N absent predicts false base, chart shows rebound to resistance then fail. The discipline is that N must be tangible product or management that changes power, not cosmetic rebrand, and high must be properly formed base breakout not extended fifth buy point, a stage warning. Together N explains why growth alone without newness stalls as market already prices known product. chapters.title: 6. S = Supply and Demand: Big Volume Demand at Key Points
chapters.summary: Supply is shares outstanding and demand is institutional volume at pivot. O'Neil quantifies that super winners had average daily volume increase 50-300 percent at breakout, illustrated as volume spike where breakout day is tallest bar in 50 days, and that float under 25 million shares at IPO amplifies moves due to scarcity, a float versus run scatter where low float winners outperformed. The chapter tells the supply story of 1990s Microsoft where float was small before splits and every breakout was on volume where demand overwhelmed supply, chart shows splits marked where float doubled but demand grew faster. The Accumulation/Distribution Rating A to E measures institutional demand over 13 weeks, illustrated where A at breakout predicts success versus D predicts failure even with same earnings. The split and secondary nuance: splits signal confidence but also increase supply, so post-split base must form anew, illustrated as split then base versus split then run failure. The case study is Home Depot 1980s where every follow-on offering was absorbed because demand exceeded supply, price rose despite issuance, chart shows offering date with volume absorption. The tool is Up/Down Volume Ratio where 1.0 means demand equals supply; 1.5 at breakout is threshold, illustrated as ratio gauge. The chapter also covers management ownership where high insider holding at 10-20 percent reduces float supply and aligns, versus low holding where supply is loose. The failure case is large float utility with breakout on average volume where supply swamps demand and base fails sixty percent. The discipline is that earnings plus chart without supply fails; S must show big volume demand at key points and manageable supply where float scarcity lets price lift. chapters.title: 7. L = Leader or Laggard: Which Is Your Stock?
chapters.summary: The leader versus laggard choice is priced in relative strength. O'Neil shows that leaders were top 10 percent Relative Strength at breakout while laggards were bottom 40 percent where cheap price reflects weak business, illustrated as RS distribution where winner cluster sits high. The chapter divides market into leaders, mediocre, and laggards using Relative Strength Rating at 80 minimum and Leader Board where IBD rates leaders A, illustrated as screen where RS 95 marks leader. Anecdote is the 2000 Cisco versus Inktomi where Cisco was assumed safety at lower RS but Inktomi with higher RS and earnings acceleration tripled before top, proving RS predicts not past performance chase. Industry leadership matters more: a leader in lagging group fails because group drags, so L requires group rank top, illustrated as group RS rank where top 40 of 197 succeed, bottom 100 fail irrespective of stock RS. The tool is choosing the best one or two in best groups, not diversifying across groups, a concentration illustration where two leaders beat ten laggards risk-adjusted. The failure case is diversifying into laggards to feel diversified — a chart shows equal weighted laggard portfolio lagging leader concentration by 15 percent annually. The discipline is to rank quantitatively and choose leader, because market pays for leadership via momentum of earnings that laggards lack; buying laggards for value is paying for problems. The closing note ties L to C and A: leadership is earnings leadership that shows in RS before price news, so RS is earnings proxy when estimates lag. chapters.title: 8. I = Institutional Sponsorship & M = Market Direction
chapters.summary: Institutional sponsorship validates liquidity and marketing where winners had 10 to 30 sponsors accumulating quarter over quarter, illustrated as sponsorship chart where sponsor count rises before price, sponsorship increasing as institutions research and buy. The chapter shows that too many sponsors at 80 plus indicates crowded top, while too few below 5 lacks demand — sweet spot 10-30, illustrated as sponsor count versus subsequent return hump. The rating Fund Ownership shows percent ownership; leader at 20-30 percent is healthy, above 50 is crowded. Market direction chapter then conditions everything: even CAN SLIM fails 75 percent when market in correction. The market direction illustration shows distribution days where volume down signals institutional selling, and follow-through day where rally on strong volume resumes uptrend — a two-signal system. Anecdote is 2008 where O'Neil's market calls turned defensive in late 2007 when distribution days stacked to six in four weeks, saving subscribers from holding leaders into bear, illustrated as S&P with distribution marks. The tool is Market Pulse daily where market in uptrend, uptrend under pressure, correction determines exposure 100, 50, 0 percent. The closing synthesis is that I checks demand validation and M checks tide; both must align with C,A,N,S,L before buying, and selling rules later chapters preserve when M turns. chapters.title: 9. When You Must Sell and Cut Every Loss & When to Take Profits
chapters.summary: The selling pair is where profits are made because buying is only half. Chapter 10 rule is cut every loss at seven to eight percent below purchase without exception, illustrated as loss tolerance chart where 8 percent loss needs 8.7 percent gain to recover but 50 percent needs 100 percent — small losses keep compounding. The discipline is mechanical: place stop at eight percent and honor it even if story intact, because thesis can be wrong and price is truth about supply. Anecdote is a subscriber who held Enron from 80 to 0 hoping, versus O'Neil holder who sold at 72 and survived. When to take profits Chapter 11 teaches to hold winner to 20-25 percent quickly, then hold for eight weeks if gain hits 20 percent in first three weeks off base — power stock holds where institutions lock. Illustrations show 20 percent profit band where scaling out misses runner, and eight-week hold box where breakout week forms support. Additional sell signals are climax top where volume spikes and price up 25 percent in two weeks, illustrated as exhaustion bar where distribution follows, and late-stage base failure. The tool is profit and loss ratio where winners should average 2.5 times losers, so cutting at eight and holding to forty achieves expectancy positive even with 35 percent win rate. The closing case is Apple 2004 where eight-week holder rode from 10 to 40 while early profit taker exited at 12, missing compounding. Together these chapters enforce that sell discipline — small loss, long winner, and hold power — is where expectancy turns positive. chapters.title: 10. Money Management & Common Mistakes and Models of Winners
chapters.summary: Money management chapter answers should you diversify, use margin, short, options, IPOs, and Nasdaq, with a conservative stance. Diversify not over twenty names; six to eight leaders concentrate without single-stock risk, illustrated as concentration versus drawdown where eight reduces variance but twenty dilutes. Margin is discouraged because eight percent stop plus leverage amplifies to sixteen quickly and forces sale at bottom, illustrated as leverage drawdown doubling. Shorting is for experts only when market correction confirmed. Options are timing instruments that decay — avoid unless hedging. IPOs are leaders per N, buy after base not first print. Twenty-one costly mistakes checklist is reproduced where top mistakes are buying low-priced laggards, averaging down, and ignoring market, each with loss case. Models of great winners chapter then shows chart library where 100 winners share base plus volume plus earnings pattern, illustrated as page of eight thumbnail charts where similarity is striking — cup-handle plus volume spike plus earnings up. The chapter tells a story of an investor who after learning patterns paper traded six months before real capital, improving win rate from 20 to 40 percent, illustrated as learning curve. Picking best market themes chapter introduces 197 groups rotation where market theme like cloud or housing cycles quarterly, illustrated as group performance heat map where top groups rotate but winners stay top during theme. How I Use IBD chapter maps SmartSelect, Stock Checkup, and Leader Board workflow daily where 15 minutes screens leaders and market pulse sets exposure, illustrated as workflow diagram. The closing synthesis is that themes plus models plus management of size and leverage turn CAN SLIM from mnemonic to daily system that fits 15 minutes alongside business analysis, not replacing it but timing it. chapters.title: 11. Important Rules, Bonus Quiz, and Success Stories
chapters.summary: The final section condenses time-tested rules into portable checklist and proves teachability. Important rules chapter lists 25 guidelines — buy at new high off proper base, cut at eight, hold eight weeks at power, don't buy on tips — reproduced as wallet card illustration. Bonus test your knowledge chapter provides eight weekly charts where readers guess breakout or failure, answers reveal that volume and base stage decide sixty percent, a scored quiz illustration. Success stories chapter shares new and advanced investors who implemented CAN SLIM with IBD tools, like a teacher who turned Rs 5 lakh to Rs 25 lakh in three years by following market pulse and eight percent stops, with verified broker statements redacted — illustration shows equity curve where drawdown stayed under 15 percent because stops worked. The stories stress that success came not from predicting Tesla but from process adherence where they missed many but let winners run to 100 percent, matching power law where one runner pays for many small losses. The closing guidance ties to earlier trilogy book where Getting Started and Advanced combine, but this volume stands alone as complete system. The final illustration places CAN SLIM letters on a circle where each feeds next and market surrounds, teaching that system beats forecast. The book ends with IBD product note on Investors.com and Digital Publishing awards, but the author's note reiterates that 100 years of winners prove winners repeat not because history repeats but because incentives — earnings, new products, institutional demand — repeat, and learning their footprints is the only proven way for an individual to manage money actively without relying on manager fees that the earlier warren buffett book argued most cannot justify. The take-home is system discipline over market prediction, practiced daily via 15-minute IBD routine that marries earnings checks with chart timing.
